title: GWEN Zero-Credential Agent Authority
pitch: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials.
about_excerpt: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials. Like Comment Story Updates 01-GWEN-Devpost-Hero-WebMCP-Connected 02-GWEN-Zero-Credential-Browser-Verification 03-GWEN-One-Time-Email-Verification 04-GWEN-Agent-Requests-Address-Authority 05-GWEN-Human-Authorization-Grant 06-GWEN-Approved-Single-Use-Commit 07-GWEN-Authority-Consumed-Audit-Receipt 08-GWEN-Qwen-Returning-User-Email Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of doing much more than answering questions. They can interact with websites, update accounts, send messages, schedule appointments, change records, and perform other real actions for people. That created a question I kept coming back to: Why should an AI need my credentials just because I want it to perform one specific action? If I ask an agent to change a delivery address, I may want it to have permission to perform exactly that change. I do not necessarily want to give it my password, a reusable API key, an OAuth token, a broad authenticated browser session, or some other credential that authorizes much more than the task I requested. GWEN started from the idea that human authentication and agent authority should be separate things . The human should authenticate as the human. The AI should receive only the smallest amount of authority necessary for the action the human actually approved. That became the central model behind GWEN: Humans authenticate. Agents receive temporary authority. And the principle behind the project: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials. WebMCP was a natural fit for this idea because it allows a website to expose structured capabilities directly to an AI agent while the application still controls exactly what those capabilities mean and when they may be used. Instead of treating an AI as another fully logged-in user, GWEN treats the AI as an agent requesting narrowly scoped authority from a human-controlled security boundary. The delivery-address change in the demo is intentionally simple. The important part is not the address. The important part is the authority model behind it. What it does GWEN is a working WebMCP security prototype that separates human authentication from agent authority . A visitor begins by using their own email address to verify control of a browser session through a temporary, one-time sign-in link. The AI never receives that sign-in link, the browser session cookie, the Gmail App Password, or the visitor's credentials. Authentication establishes that there is a verified email-controlled human session. It does not automatically authorize an AI agent to make changes. Once the browser is verified, GWEN exposes structured WebMCP capabilities. The first capability is get_gwen_capabilities . This allows an agent to discover what GWEN supports and understand the authority model without receiving human credentials. The second capability is request_address_change_authority . This allows an agent to request permission for one exact delivery-address change and provide a reason for the request. Nothing changes when the request is made. Instead, GWEN displays the exact proposed value to the human in a visible authorization panel. The human can explicitly choose Authorize GWEN or Deny . Only after the human approves the exact request does GWEN dynamically expose another WebMCP capability: commit_approved_address_change This temporary commit capability does not accept another address. The value approved by the human has already been bound on the server. For example, if the human approves: 42 WebMCP Street the AI cannot substitute: 99 Something Else Street during final execution. There is no replacement-address parameter in the final commit tool. The agent receives authority to execute the exact action the human approved . The resulting GWEN Grant is: bound to the verified human session bound to one specific action bound to the exact approved value short-lived limited to one authorized use consumed after successful execution The current WebMCP grant has a maximum lifetime of 120 seconds. After successful execution, GWEN shows: 1 of 1 consumed and: Authority remaining: NONE The temporary authority disappears. GWEN then creates a persistent, human-bound audit receipt containing the action, previous value, approved new value, grant information, number of uses, remaining authority state, timestamp, and an internal identity hash associated with the verified session. The design principle is: Temporary authority should disappear. Evidence of what happened should remain. GWEN also includes Qwen , a local AI email conversation assistant running through Ollama. Qwen's conversation authority is deliberately separate from WebMCP action authority. A verified visitor can have a normal email conversation with Qwen without giving Qwen the human's Gmail password, magic-link token, or GWEN browser-session credential. The Qwen email capability has a hard 10-minute lifetime. Replies do not extend the original deadline. Per-message capabilities are single-use. Attachments are blocked. Oversized messages are rejected. URLs are not automatically fetched. Automated reply loops are guarded against, and restarting the Qwen worker revokes outstanding Qwen email capabilities. The visible email address remains normal. The short-lived capability is carried through email reply-chain metadata instead of forcing the user to communicate through a strange tokenized email address. GWEN can also maintain compact encrypted continuity for returning verified users without keeping their old authorization alive. That created another important design rule: Memory is not authority. How we built it GWEN's primary security and authority implementation is written in Rust using Axum . I built GWEN as a solo developer and deliberately kept the architecture small enough that I could trace the complete authority path myself. A simple rule emerged while I was building it: Browser shows state. Rust decides state. Redis authorizes state. SQLite records state. Rust and Axum Rust is the main policy and application layer. It handles: email-based browser verification temporary browser sessions server-side authorization WebMCP grant creation human approval exact-value binding one-use execution persistent audit receipt creation Qwen worker supervision application lifecycle and policy enforcement The security-critical authorization decisions are made on the server. Browser JavaScript presents the state and exposes WebMCP tools, but it is not trusted to decide whether an action is actually authorized. WebMCP GWEN registers structured WebMCP tools through the browser's model-context interface using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The initial capabilities are available for agent discovery. The final commit capability only appears after the human has approved the exact requested action. This means the available WebMCP tool surface itself reflects the current authorization state. Before approval, the agent has no commit authority. After approval, the temporary commit capability appears. After successful execution, the capability disappears. The final commit tool intentionally accepts no replacement address because the human-approved value is already bound on the server. Redis GWEN uses a dedicated Redis instance at: 127.0.0.1:6387 Redis stores temporary state including: one-time login capabilities browser sessions WebMCP grants remaining authorized uses temporary Qwen email capabilities worker ownership and lease state The host also has other software using Redis on port 6379 . GWEN deliberately does not use or modify that Redis instance. Redis is a good fit for GWEN because authorization should be temporary, expiring, and capable of being consumed atomically. SQLite SQLite stores information that should persist after temporary authority disappears. That includes: WebMCP audit receipts Qwen client accounting returning-user metadata encrypted compact Qwen continuity This creates a deliberate separation: Temporary authority belongs in Redis. Persistent records belong in SQLite. Human verification GWEN uses temporary one-time email verification. The sign-in link is short-lived and single-use. The resulting browser session also has a hard 10-minute lifetime. GWEN verifies control of the email-based session used by the demonstration. It does not claim to prove a person's legal identity. The correct description is therefore email-controlled session verified , rather than claiming biometric, legal, government, or cryptographic proof of personal identity. Qwen and Ollama Qwen runs locally through Ollama using qwen3-coder:30b . Qwen is the conversation assistant. Qwen is not the source of WebMCP authorization. The Qwen worker receives trusted GWEN project grounding separately from untrusted incoming email content. That means an incoming email cannot redefine GWEN's trusted security architecture simply by containing instructions that claim to change the system's rules.
